sentences: Cross-lingual plagiarism detection studies cases in which a document in one language reuses material from a source in another language, either through direct translation or paraphrased translation[6].

sentences: Citation verification is related but more specific: it asks whether a cited source actually supports the claim made in the citing text[7].

At the same time, citationverification research is starting to explore claim-evidence modelling[10], full-text evidence retrieval[11], and large language models for assessing whether a cited claim is supported by a source passage[7].
A much closer conceptual match is the study by Zeeb and Olsson[7], which explicitly asks whether large language models can evaluate citations in scholarly documents.
They treat citation evaluation as a Solution Overview binary classification problem, using ChatGPT to assign a boolean result together with a short explanation[7].

sentences: At the same time, citationverification research is starting to explore claim-evidence modelling[10], full-text evidence retrieval[11], and large language models for assessing whether a cited claim is supported by a source passage[7].
An even more direct systems-level point of comparison is Haan’s[11] SemanticCite, which proposes citation verification through AI-powered full-text analysis and evidence-based reasoning.
The system must work with full-text documents, identify citations, retrieve and analyse source material, and produce evidence that can justify the verification result[11].
In this sense, the design is close to SemanticCite, which also approaches citation verification as an evidence-based process[11].

sentences: A widely cited taxonomy distinguishes deliberate copy-paste plagiarism, simple paraphrasing, patchwork paraphrasing, selfplagiarism, illegitimate-source plagiarism, retweet plagiarism, metaphor plagiarism, and idea plagiarism[12].
